'''Anthony Siragusa''' (May 14, 1967 – June 22, 2022), nicknamed "'''Goose'''", was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] for 12 seasons with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] and the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). After his football career, he worked as a sideline analyst for NFL games broadcast on the [[Fox Network]] from 2003 to 2015. He also hosted various shows on television, such as the home renovation program ''[[Man Caves]]'' on the [[DIY Network]].

'''Antonio Richardson''' (born December 17, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[fullback (American football)|fullback]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]], [[Minnesota Vikings]], and [[New York Jets]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was signed by the Cowboys as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1994. He played [[college football]] for the [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn Tigers]].

He is considered one of the best fullbacks in NFL history having blocked for 1,000 yards rushers in nine consecutive NFL seasons in addition to leading the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in rushing yards in 2000.  During those seasons he blocked for multiple Pro Bowl running backs including [[Priest Holmes]], [[Larry Johnson (running back)|Larry Johnson]], [[Adrian Peterson]], [[Thomas Jones (American football)|Thomas Jones]] and [[LaDainian Tomlinson]].

'''Anthony Lemont Peters''' (born April 28, 1953) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] for 10 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Cleveland Browns]] and [[Washington Redskins]].

Born in [[Pauls Valley, Oklahoma]], Peters played [[college football]] for the [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma Sooners]] at the [[University of Oklahoma]]. He and his wife, Jewell, have two children. Jewell died in 2017.  Peters' half-brother, Charles Bray, played for the [[Toronto Argonauts]] in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL).<ref name="DEA Followed Trail">[https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1983/08/07/dea-followed-a-year-long-trail-to-carlisle-and-tony-peters/27d17ce0-62c7-43a5-9952-3727105f03ab/ DEA Followed a Year-Long Trail To Carlisle--and Tony Peters] Paul Attner and Eve Zibart, ''[[The Washington Post]]'' (August 7, 1983) {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828084757/https://www.washingtonpost.com/web/20170828084757/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1983/08/07/dea-followed-a-year-long-trail-to-carlisle-and-tony-peters/27d17ce0-62c7-43a5-9952-3727105f03ab/?utm_term=.eded633b3fe3 |date=August 28, 2017 }}</ref>

Peters helped the Washington Redskins win [[Super Bowl XVII]], and earned [[Pro Bowl]] honors for the 1982 season.

On August 3, 1983, Peters was arrested by the [[Drug Enforcement Administration]] (DEA) at the Washington Redskins' training camp in [[Carlisle, Pennsylvania]], accused of having taken $3,000 from an undercover DEA agent in return for assisting in two cocaine deals in Northern Virginia in the summer of 1983.<ref name="DEA Followed Trail"/> He was one of eight men charged in a drug conspiracy to sell $115,000 worth of cocaine in the Washington area.<ref name="Peters Given Probation">[https://www.nytimes.com/1983/10/08/sports/peters-given-probation.html Peters Given Probation] ''[[The New York Times]]'' (October 8, 1983) {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240321021133/https://www.nytimes.com/1983/10/08/sports/peters-given-probation.html |date=March 21, 2024 }}</ref> On September 2, 1983, Peters pleaded guilty to conspiracy to traffic cocaine. The same day, he was suspended indefinitely by the NFL.<ref name="Peters pleads guilty">[https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/09/02/Washington-Redskins-All-Pro-strong-safety-Tony-Peters-pleaded-guilty/8722431323200/ Peters pleads guilty] Pamela Murphy, [[United Press International]] (September 2, 1983) {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20240321020318/https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/09/02/Washington-Redskins-All-Pro-strong-safety-Tony-Peters-pleaded-guilty/8722431323200/ |date=March 21, 2024 }}</ref> On October 8, 1983, Peters was fined $10,000, placed on four years' probation and ordered to perform 500 hours of community work.<ref name="Peters Given Probation"/> In June 1984, NFL Commissioner [[Pete Rozelle]] declared that Peters was eligible to resume playing for the Redskins.<ref name="NFL Surprises Redskins">[https://books.google.com/books?id=TLQDAAAAMBAJ&dq=tony+peters+cocaine+trafficking&pg=PA52 NFL Surprises Redskins, OK's Peters' Return] ''[[Jet (magazine)|Jet]]'' (June 4, 1984) {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240321021950/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=TLQDAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA52&lpg=PA52&dq=tony+peters+cocaine+trafficking&source=bl&ots=lDNK3GrmbF&sig=ACfU3U0zkVwD01B4V2fOATiLO3r_lOexwA&hl=en&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwiR4IXhooSFAxUdQkEAHY9rDGIQ6AF6BAgZEAM#v=onepage&q=tony%20peters%20cocaine%20trafficking&f=false |date=March 21, 2024 }}</ref>
Peters completed the terms of his plea deal and went on to be a successful high school football coach and social studies teacher in Texas and Oklahoma. He currently lives in Tulsa.

'''Kevin Altona''' '''"Tony"''' '''Robinson''' (born January 22, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the Super Bowl-winning [[Washington Commanders|Washington Redskins]] as a replacement member of their team during the [[National Football League Players Association#1987 strike and decertification|1987 players' strike]]. Along with other Redskins replacement players from that year, he was eventually awarded a [[Super Bowl ring]].

Robinson played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]] from 1982 to 1985. After spending his first two seasons as a backup, he guided the [[1984 Tennessee Volunteers football team|1984 squad]] to a 7–4–1 record and an appearance in the [[Sun Bowl]]. He led the [[1985 Tennessee Volunteers football team|1985 "Sugar Vols" squad]] through a difficult first half of the season, and was a [[Heisman Trophy]] candidate until blowing out his right knee during a close game against [[1985 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama]]. A few weeks after the season, he was arrested in [[Knoxville, Tennessee|Knoxville]] on charges of distributing cocaine, critically damaging his prospects in the NFL. He went undrafted in the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref name="SI">[http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1021315/index.htm "Tony Robinson, Vols Quarterback"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029201443/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1021315/index.htm |date=October 29, 2013 }}, December 11, 2000, Albert Chen, ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''. Retrieved April 5, 2010.</ref><ref name="Knox">{{Cite web |last=Keim |first=David |date=December 11, 2000 |title=Black History Month |url=http://web.knoxnews.com/web/blackhistory/stories/0225volqb.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928232402/http://web.knoxnews.com/web/blackhistory/stories/0225volqb.shtml |archive-date=September 28, 2011 |website=Knoxville News Sentinel}}</ref>

In 1987, during the strike, Robinson played in one game for the Redskins after starting replacement quarterback [[Ed Rubbert]] was injured. He led the Redskins' replacement players to an improbable 13–7 win over a [[Dallas Cowboys]] team that featured a number of players who had crossed the picket lines during the strike. His role was loosely portrayed by both [[Keanu Reeves]] and [[Michael Jace]] in the 2000 film ''[[The Replacements (film)|The Replacements]]''.<ref name=SI/><ref name=Knox/>
